pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting decimals to hundredths, understood as the SAME place-value system as whole numbers continued rightward past the point. The algorithm is identical — align by place value, compose ten hundredths into a tenth on carrying and decompose a tenth into ten hundredths on borrowing — the only new hazard is that alignment must be by the DECIMAL POINT (tenths under tenths), not by right-edging the digits, and 'ragged' decimals (3.4 + 2.78) must be equalised with a placeholder zero. Children should relate the strategy to the written method and explain WHY it works from place value.
bestPractices: Align by the decimal point; write in placeholder zeros so both numbers have the same number of places (3.4 -> 3.40)
Use base-ten blocks re-scaled (flat = 1, rod = 0.1, small = 0.01) so ten-hundredths-make-a-tenth mirrors ten-ones-make-a-ten
Estimate first (3.45 + 2.78 is about 6) to catch a misplaced point
Explicitly connect the decimal algorithm to the whole-number one - 'same exchange, new columns'
Ask the child to explain why lining up the points (not the digits) is necessary
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns with a fixed, aligned decimal point (Th... O . tenths hundredths)
commonMisconceptions: Aligns the digits by the right edge instead of by the decimal point (3.4 + 2.78 set up wrongly)
Treats the digits after the point as a separate whole number ('longer decimal is bigger', so mis-orders/mis-sets)
Loses or misplaces the decimal point in the answer
Fails to borrow across the tenths, especially with a zero (5.03 - 2.67)
Thinks appending or dropping a trailing zero changes the value

learn.summary: Add and subtract decimals to hundredths by treating the decimal point as the fixed marker of where the same place-value columns continue rightward. The written algorithm is identical to whole-number column arithmetic — align by place value, compose ten hundredths into a tenth when carrying, decompose a tenth into ten hundredths when borrowing — with one new hazard: columns must be aligned by the DECIMAL POINT (tenths under tenths), not by right-edging the digits, and 'ragged' decimals such as 3.4 + 2.78 must be equalised with a placeholder zero (3.40). Learners should estimate first to place the point, compute correctly in both directions including across a zero, and explain WHY lining up the points (not the digits) is necessary.

activities.title: Decimal exchange bench: aligning by the point and trading ten-for-one
feedback: If a learner right-edges 3.4 under 2.78 (lining the 4 under the 8), stop and insist on lining up the decimal points and inserting a placeholder zero (3.40); a highlighted empty hundredths slot can prompt this, and the re-scaled blocks show tenths sitting under tenths.
If a learner cannot take 7 hundredths from 3 hundredths in 5.03 − 2.67, model the exchange with blocks first (one whole → ten tenths, one tenth → ten hundredths) before working the digits.
If the point is lost or misplaced in the answer, anchor it with the estimate: for 3.4 + 2.78, 'about 6, so it's 6.18, not 61.8 or 0.618'.
Confirm the carry explicitly: ten hundredth-pieces fuse into one tenth-piece, which slides one column left — the same move as ten ones making one ten.
activities.rationale: A fixed-point column layout with re-scaled base-ten blocks makes 'align by the point' and the hundredths→tenths exchange concrete and connects the decimal procedure to the whole-number regrouping learners already know, supporting the standard's call to use concrete models and place-value strategies and to relate the strategy to a written method.
sourceClaims: Pupils 'add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used' (5.NBT.B.7, cluster: perform operations with decimals to hundredths).

Decimal addition/subtraction is formally established in Year 5: pupils 'practise adding and subtracting decimals, including a mix of whole numbers and decimals, decimals with different numbers of decimal places, and complements of 1' (Year 5 fractions/decimals notes and guidance).
learnerActions: Set up 3.4 + 2.78 in place-value columns with the decimal point fixed in a central column; notice that 3.4 has an empty hundredths slot (to the right of the 4, above the 8), and add the placeholder zero so it becomes 3.40 with tenths under tenths and hundredths under hundredths.

Compute 3.45 + 2.78: the hundredths total 13, so fuse ten hundredth-pieces into a single tenth-piece and carry it one column left — exactly the ones-to-tens carry already known. Record the answer 6.23.
Solve 5.03 − 2.67 by decomposing: exchange one whole into ten tenths and one tenth into ten hundredths so you can take 7 hundredths from 3 hundredths; record 2.36.
Before each calculation, estimate roughly (3.45 + 2.78 is about 6) and use the estimate to check the point is in the right place afterward.
Re-scale base-ten blocks so a flat = 1, a rod = 0.1, and a small cube = 0.01, and physically trade ten small cubes for one rod to mirror ten-ones-make-a-ten.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimals are not a new arithmetic: the point just marks where the columns keep going, and the ten-for-one exchange across every boundary (hundredths→tenths, tenths→ones) is unchanged from whole numbers. You must line up tenths under tenths and hundredths under hundredths because you can only add like to like.

activities.title: Confronting 'longer-is-larger' with ragged decimals
feedback: If a learner judges 4.11 larger than 4.9 because it has more digits, rebuild the comparison with equal places (4.11 vs 4.90) on a number line or with hundredths blocks, reading tenths and hundredths explicitly.

If a learner claims 2.78 is larger than 3.4 because it has more digits or a bigger part after the point, compare the ones first (2 ones vs 3 ones). Then rewrite with equal places (2.78 vs 3.40) and show on a number line or with blocks that 2.78 is smaller, even though 0.78 is more than 0.40. If they treat .45 and .4 as 45 and 4, compare 0.40 versus 0.45 (forty versus forty-five hundredths).
If a learner believes 6.180 differs from 6.18, establish directly that the extra zero adds zero thousandths, so the values are identical.
activities.rationale: 'Longer-is-larger' is a documented decimal misconception that is exposed specifically by ragged decimals of unequal length, and above all by cases where the longer decimal is actually the smaller one (e.g. 4.11 vs 4.9); equalising places and comparing on a shared model directly targets it, whereas a case where the longer decimal is also larger would let the misconception pass undetected.
sourceClaims: 'Longer-is-larger' is a well-documented decimal misconception in which children treat the digits after the point as a separate whole number (e.g. '4.11 is larger than 4.9 as it is longer'); it is exposed only by 'ragged' decimals of unequal length, and about half of Year 5 students make such errors. The classification traces to Sackur-Grisvard & Leonard (1985), Nesher & Peled (1986) and Resnick et al. (1989).
learnerActions: Decide which is larger, 4.11 or 4.9. Many children wrongly pick 4.11 because it 'looks longer' — but 4.9 is larger. Rewrite with equal places (4.11 vs 4.90) and read them as eleven hundredths versus ninety hundredths to see why.

Decide which is larger, 0.4 or 0.45, and whether 0.4 and 0.40 are equal or different. Then rewrite 0.4 as 0.40 (forty hundredths) to compare the same number of places directly (forty hundredths versus forty-five hundredths).
Build or mark both numbers with hundredths blocks or on a number line, lining up equal place values, and state which is larger and why.
Check the claim 'is 6.18 the same as 6.180?' and justify the answer from place value (appending a trailing zero adds zero in the next place, so the value is unchanged).

Explain in your own words why 2.78 is smaller than 3.4 even though it has more digits and a larger part after the point (0.78 vs 0.40): compare the ones first (2 < 3). Explain why you cannot judge decimal size by counting digits.
activities.intendedInsight: The digits after the point are not a separate whole number, so a 'longer' decimal is not automatically larger — 4.9 (nine tenths) is larger than 4.11 (eleven hundredths) despite having fewer digits, while 0.45 (forty-five hundredths) is larger than 0.4 (forty hundredths). You must compare the same place values. Trailing zeros do not change value because they add nothing to any place.

activities.title: Explain why the points must line up
feedback: A strong response aligns by the point using placeholder zeros, regroups correctly in both directions including across a zero, uses the estimate to place the point, and explains WHY the points must align; probe further if the learner solves equal-length items but cannot yet state the reason.

If a learner solves 3.45 + 2.78 but mis-aligns the ragged 3.4 + 2.78 or fails the borrow across the zero in 5.03 − 2.67, return to the exchange bench for that specific hazard before re-asking for the justification.
activities.rationale: Articulating why alignment follows from place value is the standard's 'explain the reasoning' strand and distinguishes procedural fluency from genuine understanding; dialogue can elicit and check this justification alongside the computation.
sourceClaims: Pupils 'add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used' (5.NBT.B.7, cluster: perform operations with decimals to hundredths).
learnerActions: Answer the question 'why must the decimal points line up — what goes wrong if they don't?' in your own words, referring to place value.
Work 5.03 − 2.67 and explain what you did to be able to take 7 hundredths from 3 hundredths (decomposing across the tenths and the zero).
Estimate 3.45 + 2.78, 3.4 + 2.78, and 5.03 − 2.67 (about 6, 6, and 2) and describe how each estimate tells you where the point belongs in the exact answer.
Transfer the reasoning to a fresh ragged or zero case you have not seen, setting it up, computing it, and justifying the alignment.
activities.intendedInsight: You can only add tenths to tenths and hundredths to hundredths, so aligning by the point keeps like place values together; estimating first lets you catch a misplaced point. Full mastery means justifying the algorithm from place value, not just following steps.

constraints: The computation is a doing skill: learners must actually set up, regroup, and compute, not merely recognise correct setups. Fill-in-the-blank or slider-estimate items can assess column setup, regrouped digits, and estimates, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of the algorithm.

Always include at least one ragged-decimal item (e.g. 3.4 + 2.78) and one borrow-across-a-zero item (e.g. 5.03 − 2.67); clean equal-length items alone confirm only the basic algorithm and hide the decimal-specific hazards.

When checking 'longer-is-larger', include at least one comparison where the longer decimal is the smaller value (e.g. 4.11 vs 4.9); a comparison where the longer decimal is also larger (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.45) does not discriminate the misconception on its own.

A tap-to-reveal worked example (tap the point to reveal 'tenths under tenths'; tap the carry to reveal ten hundredths = one tenth) is useful as fixed reference, but a fixed example cannot be re-set by the learner, so pair it with hands-on setup and computation.
Re-scaled base-ten blocks (1 / 0.1 / 0.01) are an approximation: the physical pieces have thickness and the scaling is a convention, so keep the mapping (flat = 1, rod = 0.1, cube = 0.01) explicit.
Money (pounds.pence) and metric-measure (metres.cm) contexts are helpful, but watch that the two-place convention of money does not reinforce 'always two digits after the point'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Arithmetic checked: 3.45 + 2.78 = 6.23; 3.4 + 2.78 = 6.18 (via 3.40); 5.03 − 2.67 = 2.36. Estimates about 6, 6, and 2 are consistent. These match the source's stated correct answers.

Activity 2 keeps the discriminating comparison 4.11 vs 4.9 (the longer decimal 4.11 is actually smaller), taken from the source's own misconception example. The original candidate's 0.4 vs 0.45 does not expose 'longer-is-larger' because there the longer decimal is genuinely larger; it is retained only for the trailing-zero/equal-places teaching.

Activity 2 feedback was corrected so the remediation numbers match the learner's actual error: the '2.78 bigger after the point than 3.4' confusion is rebuilt as 0.78 vs 0.40, while '.45 and .4 as 45 and 4' is rebuilt as 0.40 vs 0.45.

The source assessment's reteach note phrased a comparison as an ambiguous question ('0.4 = 0.40 = forty hundredths, larger than 0.45? No'); the intended point is that 0.40 equals forty hundredths and is NOT larger than 0.45 (forty-five hundredths). The activity states this plainly.

The original artefact-fit notes claimed a third dimension 'adds nothing' to this planar place-value work; this is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, so it is omitted rather than asserted. A 3D representation is simply unlikely to be necessary here, not proven worthless.
The 'glowing empty hundredths slot' and 'blocks fusing/sliding' are retained as optional, illustrative concrete feedback, not mandatory implementations.

The DfE Year 5 claim is kept on Activity 1 because that activity practises ragged and mixed whole/decimal cases ('decimals with different numbers of decimal places'); it supports the activity content rather than the choice of concrete representation.

probeDeeper: Roughly what should 3.45 + 2.78 come to, before you work it out exactly?
Why do the decimal points have to line up - what goes wrong if they don't?
In 5.03 - 2.67, what did you do to be able to take 7 hundredths from 3 hundredths?
Is 6.18 the same as 6.180 - how do you know?
assess.correctAnswer: 3.45 + 2.78 = 6.23 (composes ten hundredths into a tenth, ten tenths into a one). 3.4 + 2.78 = 6.18, aligning by the point with a placeholder zero (3.40). 5.03 - 2.67 = 2.36, decomposing across the tenths (and the zero). Estimates about 6, 6, and 2. Explains that the points align because you can only add tenths to tenths and hundredths to hundredths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Aligns the numbers by their right-hand digits instead of by the decimal point, so 3.4 + 2.78 lines the 4 under the 8
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on lining up the points and adding a placeholder zero (3.40); use the re-scaled base-ten bench so tenths sit under tenths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The written setup - columns do not share a vertical decimal point; answer like 3.4+2.78 = 6.22 or 0.622

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the decimal part as a separate whole number ('longer is bigger'), mis-ordering or mis-setting the numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare on a number line / with hundredths blocks; 0.4 = 0.40 = forty hundredths, larger than 0.45? No - build the direct comparison with equal places.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reasoning that 2.78 is 'bigger after the point' than 3.4, or handling .45 and .4 as 45 and 4

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot decompose across the tenths to subtract, especially with a zero, in 5.03 - 2.67
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model exchanging one whole -> ten tenths, one tenth -> ten hundredths with re-scaled blocks before the digits.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Wrong tenths/hundredths digits, or smaller-from-larger within the decimal places

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses or misplaces the decimal point in the answer, or thinks adding/dropping a trailing zero changes the value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the point with the estimate ('about 6, so it's 6.18 not 61.8'); establish 6.18 = 6.180.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer with the point in the wrong place, or 6.18 written as 6.180 believed to be different/larger

responseLevels.gap: Right-edges the digits, mis-sets ragged decimals, or loses the point; no sense of the answer's size.
responseLevels.full: Aligns by the point (using placeholder zeros), regroups correctly in both directions including across a zero, estimates to place the point, and justifies the algorithm from place value; transfers to a new ragged/zero case.
responseLevels.partial: Solves the equal-length item and can describe the steps, but mis-aligns the ragged decimal or fails the borrow across the tenths/zero, and cannot yet say WHY the points must line up.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child these to set out and solve on paper, watching how they align them: 3.45 + 2.78; 3.4 + 2.78; and 5.03 - 2.67. Ask them to estimate each answer first, and for 5.03 - 2.67 to explain why the algorithm works.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 3.4 + 2.78 is the ragged-decimal trap: a child who right-edges the digits lines the 4 under the 8 and gets nonsense, while a child who aligns by the point (and adds the placeholder zero) succeeds. 5.03 - 2.67 forces a decimal borrow across a zero. The clean 3.45 + 2.78 confirms the basic algorithm, so failures localise to the decimal-specific hazards.
